highlights.text: **To fold, fold up, or roll up** — a garment, a piece of cloth, or a written sheet
Lane judges "the day we fold up / roll up the heaven" the better rendering
Dhu-r-Rummah: "as letters are unfolded after being folded."
the Kashshāf and al-Bayḍāwī compare ثِنًى and gloss "twice sanctified" (of the valley)
highlights.note: exegetes al-Zamakhsharī (Kashshāf) and al-Bayḍāwī on ṭuwā

highlights.text: Lane reports ar-Rāghib's explanation that it signifies their destruction
Root A: a thing's flashing or gleaming.
Root B: black and white combined in a thing.
Lightning. الْبَرْق (al-barq) is the flash of a cloud (al-Khalīl)
بَرِقَ بَصَرُهُ (with kasra) = his sight was struck with bewilderment
Proverbial: "I will not do it so long as a star flashes in the sky" — i.e. so long as one rises.
Proverb: "sweeter than the water of the lightning-cloud."
Al-dam is blood, one of the bodily humours
al-Ḥuṣayn b. al-Ḥumām al-Murrī's "…on our heels the blood (al-damā) drips"
Ibn al-Aʿrābī cites the Arab saying "my blood is your blood, my hadm is your hadm", meaning "if you are wronged, I am wronged"
The Prophet answered: "Nay: the blood is the blood and the hadm is the hadm; I make war on whom you make war on and peace with whom you make peace with."
Zayd b. Thābit's ruling: "for a dāmiya, a camel"
Qatāda described smearing the child's crown with the sacrificed animal's blood
highlights.note: a report of Qatāda on the ʿaqīqa

highlights.text: Al-dawlah is time turning from hardship and misery to a state of enviable joy
It is also "the turn" in wealth — one party's share or rotation in property, explained via nawbah ("turn") and badal ("exchange")
This is the sense of Q3:140, "those days We rotate (nudāwiluhā) among people" — i.e., turn them around, from dāla, "to revolve."
illustrated by a verse of al-Rāʿī about camels reduced to eating it
dawlah is what happens between two armies — one defeats the other, then the victor is later defeated in turn
فارِط (fāriṭ) is the one who precedes
highlights.note: Ibn Sīda's core sense: going in front

highlights.text: فَرَّطَ في الشيء / فَرَّطَه — he let it go to waste and put shortcoming forward in it
الفُرُط is wrongdoing and overstepping, cited for Q 18:28, "his affair was furuṭ."
فَرَطَ عليه في القول — he overstepped and pressed forward against him in speech; cited for Q 20:45, "we fear that he will press excessively upon us or transgress."
أفْرَطَ الشيءَ — he forgot it; cited for Q 16:62, "and that they are left behind / forgotten."
Ṣakhr al-Ghayy's "that is my war-gear, and I shall not ufarriṭhu" he glosses as "I shall not squander it,"
A فَرَس فُرُط is a mare that outstrips (Labīd).
hence the Prophet's reported words, "I am your faraṭ (forerunner) at the basin."
In the prayer over a dead child, "O God, make him a faraṭ for us"
Ibn Sīda's own gloss on that verse is that the neglect is of God's affair and of the road God called to, which he identifies as affirming God's oneness and acknowledging His messenger's prophethood
the basic sense (aṣl) of ghalāʾ is rising and going beyond the measure, in everything
Ghalat al-qidr (taghlī, ghaly, ghalayān): the pot, or a jar, boiled; aghlāhā or ghallāhā: to make it boil
a saying of the ancients, "… water, and bring it to the boil", also transmitted as "make water seethe, and bring it to the boil"
A ḥadīth, "beware of ghuluww in religion", is explained as severity in religion and overstepping its bound
ʿUmar's saying "do not raise women's bridal gifts high"
a woman "spun" (غَزَلَتْ) cotton, flax, etc. — maṣdar غَزْل
The spun material/thread is called غَزِل or مَغْزُول, plural غُزُول
The dictionary cites Qur'an 16:92 — "like her who unravelled her spun thread" — as an example of the noun
نِسْوَةٌ غُزَّلٌ or غَوَازِل, illustrated with a line of pre-Islamic verse
to cleave to the ground; or to stay put, not leaving one's place; or to fall upon the breast
جَاثِم: a bird, hare, gazelle, camel, jerboa, or man clinging to the ground, staying put, or fallen on its breast
Qurʾānic evidence: فَأَصْبَحُوا فِى دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ (7:78 and parallels) — Lane's gloss: "bodies cast upon the ground"
al-Jawharī cites Bishr — "a hump, long-necked, like the جُثْمَان of the بَنِيَّة,"
Also the proverb-like phrase "he brought us broth-soaked bread heaped up like the body of a sand-grouse."
al-Bayḍāwī: extinct or motionless, and dead
Niswa / nuswa, nisāʾ, niswān / nuswān (and nisūn) serve as the plural of imraʾa (woman), though they are formed from a different word than the singular
Poetic witnesses are cited from Dukayn al-Fuqaymī and al-Shanfarā.
When moving off, the Arabs say "look to your ansāʾ", meaning check small things such as a staff, a cup or a tent-peg so they are not forgotten
Thaʿlab says God does not forget; it means they left Him and He left them, because forgetting is a kind of leaving
The Prophet disliked someone saying "I forgot (nasītu) such-and-such a verse"; he should say "I was made to forget (nussiya)"
His own reading is "or We have it left", i.e. We command you to leave it.
the underlying sense of q-ṣ-d in Arabic is resolve, turning toward, setting out and rising toward something
A separate sense: qaṣd is breaking, in any manner; some say breaking in half
al-qaṣd is "the straightness of the road."
qaṣd in a matter is "the opposite of excess."
A ṭarīq qāṣid is an easy, straight road; a safar qāṣid is an easy, short journey
cited with al-Aʿshā's line about a man whose guide in the land is the butt of a spear-shaft
He reads the Qur'anic phrase "and upon God is the qaṣd of the road" as meaning that it is upon God to make the straight road to Him plain by proofs and demonstrations
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 16:9

highlights.text: He cites the ḥadīth "no moderate man (muqtaṣid) has become poor, nor will he."
Al-qāb is the section of a bow between the hand-grip and the curved tip; every bow has two qābs
qāb/qīb also just means "a measure" or "amount" — as in phrases like "the measure of a bow" — and "qāba qawsayn" is glossed elsewhere as simply "the length of two bows."
A well-known proverb runs "qā'iba (freed) from qūb" or "qāba from quwab."
A Bedouin of Banū Asad tells a merchant hiring his escort: once I get you to such-and-such a place, "an egg is freed from its chick"
some scholars read it as short for "qābay qaws" — two qābs of a single bow, with the wording inverted
raḍiya, yarḍā (to be pleased)
Al-Ṣiḥāḥ treats riḍwān, ruḍwān and marḍāh as equal to riḍā
Qur'anic fī ʿīshatin rāḍiya is explained as marḍiyya, "pleasing", that is, possessed of satisfaction
raḍītu l-shayʾa and irtaḍaytuhu: I approved the thing, so it is marḍiyy
Zuhayr: "They are between us, and they are acceptable (riḍan), and they are just (ʿadl)."

"God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him" (raḍiya llāhu ʿanhum wa-raḍū ʿanhu) is interpreted as: God was pleased with their deeds, and they were pleased with what He recompensed them with
highlights.note: unnamed exegetical reading of the Qur'anic phrase

highlights.text: means he sat or lay in wait for someone in the road, or he watched and waited for him
رَصَد, and the nouns of place مَرْصَد, مِرْصَاد and مُرْتَصَد, denote a road or way, and specifically a place where one lies in wait for an enemy
Q 9:5 وَاقْعُدُوا لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍ — "lie in wait for them on every road"
Q 89:14 إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِالْمِرْصَادِ — "your Lord is in the way," i.e. on the road you travel, so that no act of yours escapes Him (Msb)
ارصد لَهُ (marked by Lane as figurative) — he prepared or made ready something for someone: an army for battle, a horse for a charge, money for a debt
ʿAdī's verse: وَإِنَّ المَنَايَا لِلرِّجَالِ بِمِرْصَدِ — "deaths lie in ambush for men," so that men cannot slip past them.
al-Aʿmash reported as taking المرصاد here as a name of three bridges behind the ṣirāṭ — on one security, on another mercy, on the third the Lord
explained as watchers set over an angel bearing a revelation, so that no jinnī could overhear it and pass it to diviners, who would then relay it to men and so rival the prophets
Rafraf is thin brocade, and green cloths made into furnishings for sitting-places (al-Muḥkam: spread out), unit noun rafrafa
al-Muʿaṭṭal al-Hudhalī, of a lion: "he has a thicket whose hidden depths people do not feel safe from; he has made a preserve of its trailing growth, long and lank, and of castor plants"
Ibn al-Athīr reports Ibn Masʿūd on Q 53:18 ("he truly saw, of the signs of his Lord, the greatest"): "he saw a green rafraf that blocked the horizon", glossed as a spread, or a bed-covering
al-Farrāʾ reports that some took these to be the meadows of the Garden and others beds and spreads
Sibṭ: the child of one's child; in al-Muḥkam, the child of either son or daughter
Al-Azharī: the asbāṭ among Banū Isḥāq correspond to the qabāʾil among Banū Ismāʿīl
Quṭrub: the singular of asbāṭ is sibṭ, used invariably for one, one female, and a plural group, and it means "group" (firqa)
Ḥassān's line: "Many a maternal uncle of mine — open-handed on the bitterly cold day."
The ḥadīth: "al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn are the two sibṭs of the Messenger of God."
Al-Zajjāj: the sense is "we divided them into twelve groups (firqa), asbāṭ,"
السَّلّ is defined as extracting something and bringing it out with gentleness (رِفْق)
highlights.note: Zabīdī's core sense: to draw out gently

highlights.text: Defined as whatever is extracted from something; a drop of seed is called man's sulāla
انْسَلَّ / تَسَلَّلَ = to slip out of a crowd, to leave stealthily and unnoticed
The author connects the Qur'anic يَتَسَلَّلُونَ مِنكُمْ لِوَاذًا [24:63] to this sense, citing al-Layth that يتسللون and ينسلّون mean the same thing
Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr's famous line calls the Prophet "a sword of God, drawn" (سُيُوفِ اللهِ مَسْلُولُ)
highlights.note: Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: The proverb "she pinned her own fault on me and slipped away" (رمتني بدائها وانسلت) is traced to a specific pre-Islamic anecdote about co-wives
a report from ʿIkrima glosses it as the fluid drawn from the back, supported by Qur'an 32:7–8, where God moves from "clay" to "a sulāla of despised water" — taken as God's own gloss of the term
highlights.note: a report of ʿIkrima on Q 23:12

highlights.text: Qatāda and al-Farrāʾ instead take it as "Adam was drawn out of clay, hence named sulāla."
highlights.note: exegetes Qatāda and al-Farrāʾ on Q 23:12

highlights.text: السُّرَى (al-surā), formed like الهُدَى, is night-travel
أَسْرَى (verbal noun إسْراء) means the same as سَرَى; the alif-form is Ḥijāzī, and the Qurʾān uses both
a rivulet — a small stream running to palm trees (Labīd's verse describing palms on a stream). By this Q 19:24 is explained, "your Lord has placed beneath you a sariyy."
Labīd's line "the night-journey has grown long" uses a masculine verb, evidence for masculine treatment
Ḥassān b. Thābit's verse pairs both forms of the verb
highlights.note: Ḥassān b. Thābit, lived into Islam

highlights.text: ʿAlam al-Dīn al-Sakhāwī, in his tafsīr — the distance would ordinarily take at least forty days, so "in a night" is the point of wonder
Jurists say سَرَى الجُرْحُ إلى النَّفْسِ — the wound's effect continued until death resulted
sāla / yasīlu, verbal nouns sayl and sayalān, said of water or of a thing: it flowed
Al-Zabīdī concludes that sayl is originally a verbal noun that became a name for water that reaches you although its rain did not fall where you are
Qur'anic evidence: "the torrent bore a swelling foam," and "We sent upon them the sayl of the ʿarim."
Al-Zabīdī cites the Qur'anic "and We made a spring of molten copper flow for him," glossing asalnā as "We made it run,"
as in al-Aʿshā's line about a castaway with the floods running over him
"The torrent swept them away, and the sea surged with us" — a proverb meaning they met a hard trial and the speakers a harder one
زَلَّ is used of an arrow sliding off a coat of mail and of a person slipping off a rock; equivalent to زَلِقَ
highlights.note: Ibn Manẓūr's core sense: to slip

highlights.text: The base sense is to shake a thing violently; زَلْزَلَ اللهُ الأَرْضَ … فَتَزَلْزَلَتْ
Some derive زَلْزلة from زَلَل in opinion: زُلْزِل القومُ = they were turned from steadiness and fear was cast into their hearts
تَزَلْزَلت نفسُه = his soul quaked/recoiled in his breast at death (verse of Abū Dhuʾayb
Abū Isḥāq: the meaning is "shaken with a violent shaking"
Thaʿlab's, that he made them slip in judgement/opinion
The prayer "O God, rout the Confederates and shake them" is read as making their affair unsettled and unstable
means "I set it apart, I sorted it out from something else."
highlights.note: Ibn Manẓūr's core sense: to separate

highlights.text: The Qur'anic لو تَزَيَّلوا ("had they been separated") is glossed لو تَمَيَّزوا — "had they been set apart from one another."
زَيَّلَه فَتَزَيَّل — all meaning "he divided it, and it became divided."
al-Mutalammis, "O Ḥārith, even were our bloods stirred together, they would separate until no blood touched blood"
Abū Dhuʾayb, "towards litters like dawm-palms, in which there is a drawing apart, and a swaying of interlaced loads."
A ḥadīth is cited, خالِطوا الناسَ وزايِلُوهم ("mix with people and part from them"), explained as parting from them in acts that do not please God and His Messenger.
core sense of force and severity
highlights.note: Ibn Manẓūr's root sense: force and severity

highlights.text: Al-Layth glosses it as (a) torment/punishment and (b) intensity in war
"lā tabtaʾis" = do not grieve or complain
the blame-verb (opposite of niʿma, the praise-verb)
al-baʾsāʾ and al-mabʾasa carry the same sense (shāhid from Bishr b. Abī Khāzim)
the proverb "ʿasā l-ghuwayru abʾusan" ("perhaps the little cave holds disasters")
Al-Zajjāj glosses Qurʾanic "baʾsāʾ wa-ḍarrāʾ" as hunger, versus affliction in wealth and lives
glossed by various reports as Banū Ḥanīfa, or Hawāzin, or Persia and Rome
"mā fatiʾtu" / "mā fataʾtu adhkuruhu" = "I did not cease to remember [it/him]"
highlights.note: تَفْتَؤُا, once: you will not cease

highlights.text: The Qurʾānic line "By God, you will not cease (tafta'u) remembering Joseph" (12:85) is cited as exactly this omitted-negation case.
A poetic citation (Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya) uses the verb the same way, describing a beast that "never ceases" night-travel.
originally means to shout «وَاغَوْثاهُ» — "O for help!"
highlights.note: the word's origin: a cry for help

highlights.text: istighātha is the seeking of ghawth, defined here as deliverance from hardship and calamity, and aid in getting free of distress
اسْتَغَاثَنِي فُلانٌ فَأَغَثْتُهُ — "he sought my help and I helped him,"
highlights.note: the Qur'an's verb of calling for help

highlights.text: al-Tahdhīb makes it a clan of al-Azd, citing Zuhayr: "you fear the archers of Ghawth from every lookout."
highlights.note: Zuhayr, pre-Islamic; on the clan name Ghawth

highlights.text: the underlying idea is "breaking" (أصل الهضم الكسر)
haḍamahu / ihtaḍamahu / tahaḍḍamahu = he wronged, usurped from, or oppressed him
haḍīm = soft/tender
folded/compressed within its calyx-covering (the standard gloss)
Ṭarafah is cited praising a man's slender waist this way
Imruʾ al-Qays's famous line ("she leaned toward me, slender of flank") is cited
haḍīm = whose parts fold into one another
al-hudhud proper is the well-known bird (the hoopoe); its call is hadhada or hadīl
One poetic image compares a broken-winged hudhud to a man whose baggage-camels were seized by a tax-collector.
Al-Muḥkam calls it the largest size of bowl; al-Rāghib specifies it as a food-vessel
Plural jifān is attested in the Qur'an (34:13, "basins like reservoirs")
A verse of Ḥassān is cited for "the gleaming bowls."
highlights.note: Ḥassān b. Thābit, lived into Islam

highlights.text: j-r-r as one root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): drawing a thing out and dragging it
Laqīṭ's line: "she has trailed the rope of a skittish mount over what is between us, so that we see from her neither plain despair nor hope"
Hence the proverb for someone who opposes the group's opinion and then comes round to it: "he struggled with the jurra, then made peace with it"
The ḥadīth "no ṣadaqa on al-ibil al-jārra" refers to camels drawn by their reins and led
kabba (Form I) means to tip something over or throw it down on its face
"fa-kubkibū fīhā hum wa-l-ghāwūn" — "and they were hurled/tumbled into it, they and those who went astray" (Q 26:94–95)
its literal sense, they note, is repeated inkibāb: falling face-first over and over until coming to rest at the bottom
A proverb — "like the one who sells the kubba for the hubba [wind]"
Ibn Masʿūd warns against "the kubba of the market, [which] is the kubba of Satan" — its crush/crowd.
The root's core image is things piling up, clumping, or bonding into a fixed mass
highlights.note: the entry's summary of the root sense

highlights.text: the ordinary word for a seat, plural karāsī (also pronounced kirsī)
kursī is simply what the Arabs know as the "chairs/thrones of kings."
al-akārīs are bands or groups of people (singular kirs, plural akrās, then akārīs as a further plural), used by Abū ʿAmr and illustrated in verse by Rabīʿa ibn al-Jaḥdar
Some tafsīrs equate kursī with God's "knowledge"
another view that kursī is God's "power by which He sustains the heavens and earth"
the soundly transmitted report from Ibn ʿAbbās is instead that "the kursī is the place of the [two] feet,"
highlights.note: a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, per al-Azharī

highlights.text: makkana / amkana someone min al-shayʾ = to give him power over it
al-mukna (ḍamma) = power, capability
some theologians define it instead as an "accident" — the containing relation between an enclosing body and what it encloses
Among the Sufis, al-tamkīn is the station of being firmly rooted and settled in uprightness
al-masāʾ is the opposite of morning (al-ṣabāḥ), and al-imsāʾ, entering the evening, the opposite of al-iṣbāḥ
Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt praises God "at our evening and at our morning"
In a line of Imruʾ al-Qays a young woman lights the dark like the lamp at a secluded monk's mumsā, meaning the cell where he spends the evening
Al-Azharī stresses that qaylūlah/maqīl really means resting at midday, not necessarily sleeping
Taqayyala = he slept at midday
al-maqīl (also al-maqāl) = the resting-place itself
a line from Umm Taʾabbaṭa Sharran contrasting qayl with secret nursing
'Take your midday rest, for devils do not' (i.e. rest)
"head / topmost part."
رَأْس is the head of anything, hence its highest point
Poetic witness (Imruʾ al-Qays): driving horses "down from the tops of the mountains."
A ḥadīth about "taking from the head while fasting" is explained as referring to kissing.
highlights.note: a hadith, as explained by the entry

highlights.text: "the raʾs (head) of unbelief is from the east" (taken as a pointer to the Dajjāl or eastern leaders of misguidance)
the root's original meaning is **pelting with stones**, later extended to all the above
The epithet rajīm for Satan is explained by any of three: cursed, reviled, or driven off.
This underlies {وجعلناها رجوماً للشياطين}: the *shuhub* (meteors) are missiles against the demons
The Ṣiḥāḥ ties this to {رجماً بالغيب} (guessing at the unseen)
a conjectured report whose truth cannot be pinned down (verse of Zuhayr)
specifically stoning the married adulterer to death
Al-Zabīdī reads the Qurʾanic {لتكونن من المرجومين} as "those killed in the ugliest way."
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of a verse

highlights.text: An alternative reading: rujūm = the guesses of astrologers, and "demons" = the demons among humankind.
Ibn al-Athīr says the root sense is hitting with the foot, as a mount is struck
glosses rakḍ as "moving the leg," citing Q38:42, where Job is told, "Strike (urkuḍ) with your foot — here is a cool bathing place and drink."
"he rakaḍa" = he fled
A separate verse (attributed to Aws b. Ghalfāʾ) uses the same word-shape to describe a thoroughbred mare that kicks the ground galloping (rakkāḍa)
of a woman, the swish of her skirts and anklet against her legs as she walks (illustrated by al-Nābigha)
a ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās describing the blood of istiḥāḍa as either "a persistent vein" or "a rakḍa from Satan."
Al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ both read it as fleeing/being routed from the punishment.
highlights.note: exegetes al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ on Q 21:12

highlights.text: a garment, head of hair, or coat of mail "grew long, reaching the ground" (al-Layth)
He defines dirʿ sābigha as a coat of mail long and wide enough to drag on the ground, or reaching to the ankles
highlights.note: سَٰبِغَٰت, once: full coats of mail

highlights.text: asbagha Allāhu ʿalayhi al-niʿma — "God made the favor complete/full for him."
ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib addressing his father's widow in a pre-Islamic Jāhiliyya poem (his "adornment" is his sword, hers is a sābigha)
Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī (armor made by Dāwūd or by the legendary king Tubbaʿ)
highlights.note: Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī, lived into Islam

highlights.text: asbagha al-wuḍūʾ — "he performed the ablution thoroughly," reaching every required spot and giving each limb its due
The verb is سَقَطَ / يَسْقُطُ / سُقُوطاً; the participle is سَاقِط
أَسْقَطَ = to make something fall. تَسَاقَطَ = to fall in continuous succession.
Ibn Sīda first gives the general sense "he slipped and erred,"
illustrated by a verse of al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī about wild animals huddling in the shade
al-Fārisī takes it as striking one's palms on one's hands out of regret
gathering its branches under the concealing of a thing, and under a thing's pure part and settled place
Asrartu al-shayʾ means "I kept the thing secret," the opposite of aʿlantuhu, "I declared it."
From it comes **al-surūr, gladness**, "because it is a state free of sorrow."
Al-sarīr is a couch, plural surur and asirra
Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ speaks of noble offspring "through the unmixed sirr of lineage."
Al-Aʿshā has "look at a hand and its lines."
decorative patterning/embroidery
a horse's or other animal's color — specifically a patch that differs from its main coat (al-Ṣiḥāḥ)
The phrase "lā shiyata fīhā" (no shiyah in her) is explained here as: no color in her differs from the rest of her coat.
Proverb: "he keeps on walking and informing" — a pun on mashy (walking) and washy.
tawashshā fīhi l-shayb = grey hair appeared in his hair (= al-shiyah), with a supporting verse
خَسَا (khasā) means "odd, unpaired."
خَسَأَ الكلبَ (verbal nouns خَسْأ, خُسوء) — he drove the dog off, chased it away
It means the driven-away (مطرود) and the distanced (مبعد); it can also carry the sense of the abased and contemptible (صاغِر قَمِئ)

the well-wish to one wearing new clothes, أَبْلَيْتَ جَديداً وتَمَلَّيْتَ حَبِيباً ("wear out the new, long enjoy a loved one")
gathering together in a thing, plus smallness and lightness (nimbleness)
نَمْل (naml) is the plural of نَمْلَة (namla), "an ant."
أُنْمُلَة (unmula), plural أَنَامِل (anāmil) — the tips of the fingers.
core meaning is one thing facing or confronting another (muwājaha)
qibalan means "face-to-face"
qabiltu al-shayʾa qabūlan = "I accepted the thing."
the proverb "he doesn't know qabīl from dabīr" (front from back)
a single lineage can also be called qubayl (Labīd cited)
al-qird (the monkey)
"So-and-so is more abject than the monkey and the tick — lower than the tick."
al-Ḥuṭayʾa says even Banū Kulayb's "tick" is hard to draw out and manage
dividing/apportioning
Qasama (and intensive qassama) = to divide a thing into parts
Al-qasam = an oath (plural aqsām). Aqsama bi-llāh = he swore by God.
Taqāsama al-qawm = they bound each other by mutual oath — as in Q 27:49, "They said, swear a mutual oath by God."
Labīd applies it to God: "Be content with what the Sovereign apportioned; its Divider has apportioned our livelihood."
pointing to three root meanings, which he considers related to one another
The rabb is the owner, the creator and the master, and also the one who sets a thing right.
A man's rabīb is his wife's son, and the rābb is the one who takes charge of the rabīb's affairs.
In ʿAlqama's line "my ribāba passed to you; before you, lords (rubūb) had charge of me, and I was lost,"
رُمَّان (rummān) is the pomegranate, the fruit of a well-known fruit tree
whose core sense is breadth, open space, and steady movement
He traces the whole family back to الرِّيح (al-rīḥ, "wind")
late afternoon/evening, named from the wind (rawḥ) that usually rises after midday
camels رَاحَتْ (came home) and أَرَحْتُهَا (I brought them home), tied to Qurʾān 16:6 {when you bring them home}
A verse of Abū Kabīr uses يَرَاحُ for feeling the cold breeze.
A line of al-Aʿshā using الرَّوَح of birds is read either as "scattered birds" or "birds returning to their nests."
الرُّوح as Gabriel (Jibrīl) — cited from Qurʾān 26:193
The Ramadan تَرْوِيحَة is named from the congregation's resting (istirāḥa) after every four rakʿas.
a core idea of sweeping/clearing away, which then yields "uncovering," "travel," and "making plain."
highlights.note: editor's summary of the root sense

highlights.text: Travel (السَّفَر), the opposite of staying home (الحَضَر).
سَفَرَ / أسْفَرَ الصُّبْح = "dawn grew light"
أسْفَرَ وجهُهُ = "his face beamed."
السَّفَرَة = scribes (singular سافِر; said to be Nabataean سافرا)
Zuhayr called a wild cow مُسافِرة, "roaming."
a camel or she-camel strong for travel (citations from al-Namir b. Tawlab and al-Akhṭal)
highlights.note: al-Namir b. Tawlab, lived into Islam

highlights.text: and specifically the recording angels who tally deeds
is the light of fire and of lightning; cited from Qur'an 24:43, "the sanā of its lightning almost takes away sight,"
By extension السَّنَة means a drought-year: "the sana struck them" = the year of famine
سَنَا البَرْق means the lightning gave light (with a verse of Tamīm ibn Muqbil)
highlights.note: Tamīm ibn Muqbil, lived into Islam

highlights.text: In al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī's line comparing a woman's smile to "the sanā of musk," Ibn Sīda notes sanā could mean this plant (mingled with musk) OR "light,"
The core idea is fire and its blazing.
The usual rule: the ḍamma-form (wuqūd) is the verbal noun, the fatḥa-form (waqūd) the firewood.
transitive kindling: أَوْقَدَها (awqada), وَقَّدَها (waqqada), استَوْقَدَها, تَوَقَّدَها
three fundamental senses: (1) one thing coming after another and taking its place; (2) "behind," the opposite of "in front"; (3) change or alteration
al-khalaf: what comes afterward, a successor.
"This is behind me (khalfī)" vs. "this is in front of me (qudāmī)"
al-khilāf in a promise = breaking/failing it
"People differed (ikhtalafa)" / "people are khilfa (at variance)" → assigned to the FIRST sense: each sets aside another's view and puts himself in its place
a line of Labīd on danger "behind her and before her" is cited
a line of al-Aʿshā on a broken tryst
the Prophetic saying that the fasting person's changed mouth-odor (khulūf) is more fragrant to God than musk
willing obedience. al-Ṭawʿ is the opposite of karh: compliance as against coercion
highlights.note: Root sense: willing compliance, not coercion

highlights.text: The verb ṭāʿahu (yaṭūʿuhu) and ṭāwaʿahu = "obeyed, complied with"
to have the power/capacity for something
"fa-man taṭawwaʿa khayran fa-huwa khayrun lahu" ("whoever volunteers good, it is better for him")
al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī on a most compliant lord
The idiom "you shall do it ṭawʿan or karhan" = willingly or unwillingly
"to appear": بَدَا (badā) = a thing appeared or became manifest
The causative abdā = to make [something] appear
Desert / nomadic life (opposite of settled life, al-ḥaḍar): the nouns al-badw, al-bādiya, al-badāh, al-bidāwa, al-badāwa
badā al-qawm badāʾan = the people went out to the desert
illustrated by al-Shammākh's line ("…a change of mind about that she-camel has occurred to you")
In Ibn Aḥmar's line, badw is either a collective noun for bādin (paralleling rākib/rakb) or means "desert life" itself
a door, gate, or place of entrance
as in Ibn-Muqbil's verse "a frequent enterer of doors"
fārih used on its own: skilled/expert at a thing (al-ḥādhiq bi-l-shayʾ)
A citation from al-Nābighah uses al-fārihah for a singing-girl and the gifts accompanying her (per Ibn Sīdah's gloss)
al-Azharī reports Bedouin usage of jāriya farihah for a beautiful young woman
Deceiving: من غرّك منه = "who deceived you about it, who led you into a blind spot."
ما غرّك به؟ = "what emboldened you against him?" — cited alongside the Qur'an, ما غرّك بربك الكريم (Q 82:6), "what emboldened/deceived you concerning your generous Lord."
Proverb: "more heedless than a gazelle on a moonlit night" — it mistakes the moonlight for day, ventures out, and is eaten.
a line of al-Namir uses a "bond that became ghurar," i.e. not to be trusted
Ibn Fāris treats j-d-d as having three separate root meanings: greatness, fortune and cutting.
He cites "exalted is the jadd of our Lord" (Q 72:3) for this sense.
A jadīd garment is one its weaver has "just cut".
A judda is a streak or track, and also the stripe on a donkey's back.
Proverbs: "whoever travels the level ground is safe from stumbling" and "gently, they are coming up onto the level ground".
A verse of al-Aʿshā speaks of "the doubtful well" that no rain has reached.
Ibn Fāris cites the Prophet's supplication, "the jadd of the one who has jadd does not avail him against You".
Anas ibn Mālik said that a man who had recited Sūrat al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān "became jadd among us", meaning he grew great in their hearts.
highlights.note: saying of a Companion, Anas ibn Mālik

highlights.text: jafā l-shayʾ / tajāfā: a thing failed to stay attached to its place
highlights.note: Root sense: not staying in place

highlights.text: jafā janbuhu ʿan al-firāsh / tajāfā: his side pulled away from the bed, recoiled, did not rest on it

Ibn Sīda records three exegetical views on what this describes: (a) they used to pray at night; (b) they did not sleep through the ʿatamah (late-night) prayer; (c) they used to pray voluntarily between maghrib and the later ʿishāʾ
Asked what she will do on a rainy night, the she-goat answers: her wool is fine, her hide thin, and her tail is jafāʾ (too scant/inadequate to shelter her)
Ibn Fāris says that j-l-l has three root meanings (uṣūl): greatness, one thing enveloping another, and sound.
The jalāl of God is His greatness, and He is dhū al-jalāl wa-l-ikrām, "Possessor of greatness and honour".
The expression faʿaltu dhāka min jalālika, "I did that out of your jalāl", is explained as "out of your greatness in my breast"
Of water, blood and the like: to flow.
Of a ship: to sail. Hence al-jāriya = a ship — a descriptive term that became a fixed name for it — citing the Qurʾanic "in the jāriya" and "the jawārī raised up on the sea."
Ibn Sīda notes that in a verse of Abū Dhuʾayb the "running" is a man's charge into battle, not a horse's gallop
Ibn Sīda reads the Qurʾanic "al-jawārī" (Q 81) as the stars.
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 81

highlights.text: a sound root with a single core meaning: covering and concealing
The sower/tiller is a kāfir because he covers the seed with soil.
Likewise kufrān al-niʿma is denying and concealing a blessing (ingratitude).
In poetry al-kāfir is glossed as the place where the sun sets, or as the sea (the setting sun "casts its hand into kāfir").
istakāna — "to submit, to become humbled/lowly."
Al-Azharī connects the Qur'anic phrase "fa-mā-stakānū li-rabbihim" (Q23:76, "they did not submit to their Lord") to this root.
Abū Saʿīd cites the causative akāna ("to subdue, humble someone"), with a verse of grim consolation ("wounds that subdue him do not heal me — only his wives' widowhood will")
al-mashy, "walking" (verb mashā yamshī), well known
al-mashshāʾ is one who goes about among people spreading calumny (namīma)
Illustrated by verses of al-Ḥuṭayʾa, al-Shammākh (ostriches walking "as Christians walk in leather boots"), and others
cutting away, paring, hewing
naḥata al-jabal = he cut into the mountain, treated as the same sense.
al-Naḥāʾit, a set of well-known wells, named by a description that stuck because they were hewn (cut) out
he tied or knit the thing together and made it firm and strong
قِنْطَارٌ (qinṭār) — a large measure of wealth. Described broadly as a standard of weight or measure; or an indeterminate quantity; or simply a large, unspecified mass of property, heaped up.
مُقَنْطَرٌ (muqanṭar) — gathered into one aggregate; heaped up, made complete (synonym مُكَمَّل)
The phrase قَنَاطِيرُ مُقَنْطَرَةٌ is explained as "much wealth heaped together" (Jalālayn at Q 3:14)
al-Rajaz is the quivering of a camel's leg when it tries to rise before it straightens out
(a) punishment, torment
(b) the worship of idols, and it is said, shirk of any kind — the reasoning being that one who worships other than God is in doubt and inner disturbance
سَكَنَ (سُكُونًا): a moving thing coming to rest, its motion departing
سَكَنَ الدَّارَ (to dwell in a place)
سَكَن = that which one turns to for rest — family, wealth, and the like
miskīn also denotes the abased and subdued, even a wealthy person; cf. 2:61, where "abasement and مَسْكَنَة (wretchedness)" are stamped on a people.
waḍana something = he folded part of it over another part, doubling it.
a sarīr mawḍūn ("doubly woven couch") is the term the author links directly to the Qur'anic phrase "ʿalā sururin mawḍūna" (Q. 56:15)
Al-Aʿshā's verse describes "the weave of Dāwūd" (i.e. mail armor) driving a caravan.
He gives the core sense as fulfilling and completing
وَفَى بالعَهْدِ = to keep faith with a covenant (verbal noun wafāʾ)
أَوْفَى/وَفَّى الرجلَ حقَّه = paid him his due in full; tawaffā = took it in full; istawfā = left nothing of it
الوَفَاة = death; تَوَفّاهُ اللهُ = God took him.
With a shawāhid from Abū Dhuʾayb: أُوْفى here means to look out over a rise of ground and come to it
Ibn Sīda cites al-Zajjāj's two readings: (a) the angels of death take them, and they confess their disbelief as they die; or (b) the angels of punishment take them
khaṭaʾ is "deviation from the right direction."
Al-khāṭiʾ is one who deliberately aims at sin — hence "none eat it but the khāṭiʾūn" (69:36–37).
khaṭīʾa is most often used of something not itself intended, where an original aim is the cause that generates the act
Illustrated by the verse "you meant to harm me but dragged in my delight,"
This is the sense in the reports "error and forgetfulness are lifted from my community" and "whoever exercises judgement and errs still has a reward,"
Al-Rāghib divides the causing act into two: a forbidden cause (drinking the intoxicant — the resulting error is not excused) and a non-forbidden cause (shooting at game)
ease / being made easy. The verb (yasara / yasira, and its forms tayassara, istaysara, and the causatives yassara and yāsara) means to make a thing easy or smooth.
An "easy matter" (amr yasīr) is one that is not hard; cited with the Qur'anic "with hardship comes ease."
a matter "made easy" is maysūr, cited with the Qur'anic "a gentle word."
The verb yasara means to cast the divining/gambling arrows (qidāḥ) and to play at maysir
cited with Abū Duʾād's line about readying a swift, sharp-speared horseman
Labīd (giving a "fat maysir-portion" to neighbors)
He cites the Qurʾanic فأَخَذَتْهم الصَّيْحةُ ("the ṣayḥa seized them"), glossing ṣayḥa here as the punishment.
highlights.note: ṣayḥa as the punishing blast, 13 times

highlights.text: Shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays: "Leave off the plunder over whose fringes an alarm was cried…"
from one core idea: strength and prominence/coming-into-view
ẓahara (ظَهَرَ), verbal noun ẓuhūr, participle ẓāhir — a thing becomes uncovered and comes into the open
ẓuhūr = victory, being uppermost. Cited: Qur'an al-Ṣaff 61:14, {fa-aṣbaḥū ẓāhirīn} ("so they became prevailing/uppermost")
ẓahīr — as though he braces his back against yours
Supported by a verse of Abū Dhuʾayb ("a complaint whose disgrace passes away from you").
one root meaning "the beginning / outset of a thing,"
البُكْرة (bukra) is the early morning (pl. bukar)
الإبكار means "early morning" (paralleling iṣbāḥ for "morning")
al-Khalīl — a bikr is a woman never touched (a virgin)
A bikr vine is one that has borne for the first time (verse of al-Aʿshā).
proverb: "the strongest of people is a firstborn son of two firstborns."
One core meaning, to which all branches trace back (even if some seem distant): the mixing/variegation of colors, one against another.
al-buqʿah (per al-Khalīl) — a piece of land visually distinct from what's beside it
illustrated with lines of poetry by Bishr and by al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḥumām on the clan's smallness and its standing
highlights.note: Bishr and al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḥumām, pre-Islamic

highlights.text: A proverb, "a donkey's fatness saved it in al-Baqīʿ," plays on the irony of being spared because of the very trait that should have marked it for use.
Ibn Fāris states this root has a single core meaning: plant growth.
al-Khalīl defines baql as plant growth that counts as neither a small shrub nor a large, coarse shrub.
A line of poetry by Abū al-Ṭamaḥān uses bāqil descriptively of a lush place.
The Qur'anic attestation cited is حُجَّتهم داحِضة, "their argument is dāḥiḍa" (slipping / void).
أَدْحَضَ حُجَّتَه = he nullified it, and أَدْحَضَها اللّهُ of God
Ṭarafa's line — "he swerved as the camel swerves away from the slippery ground" — as the attestation for the sukūn form daḥḍ
one governing idea: the back, rear, or end of a thing — the opposite of its front (qubul)
الدُّبُر — the hind or back part, opposite of the front.
قَطَعَ اللهُ دَابِرَهُم (Qur'anic phrasing) — cut off the last remnant of them.
to manage an affair by looking to how its end (dubur) will turn out
furrows or plots of tilled land (with a verse of Bishr)
freeing a slave "ʿan dubr," i.e. to take effect after the owner's death ("he is free after my death")
al-kashṭ is "lifting/removing a thing from [another] thing that had covered it" — e.g. stripping hide off a camel's hump or a flayed carcass (per Kitāb al-ʿAyn).
to kashaṭa a covering off something, a hide off a slaughtered camel, or a saddle-cloth off a horse's back — meaning to tear it off, pull it away, and uncover what's beneath.
Al-Zajjāj: torn/uprooted away, like a roof torn off (a dialectal spelling qushiṭat, with qāf, carries the same sense).
لُؤْلُؤَة (luʾluʾa) means a pearl (durra).
Ibn al-Aḥmar's line describes a glossy white animal as لُؤْلُؤان اللون ("pearl-coloured"), brought to water by the dew while a cold star withdrew.
one sound root whose various branches all trace back to a single core idea — whiteness
Māʾ milḥ and (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, with a supporting verse about the water of Qaww) māʾ māliḥ are both attested for "salty water."
Illustrated with a verse by Nuṣayb lamenting that his once-sweet drinking water had turned salty, adding to his suffering.
each built on the image of the nahr as the body's foremost, confronting point
From this comes nahara, "to slaughter [a camel]" — properly, to stab it at the nahr (distinct from dhabh, cutting the throat).
A verse of 'Alqama pictures dawn "confronted" by a bright star.
A proverb, "the thief stole, then intahara," describes someone compounding a wrong with a further drastic act.
A violent wind (*ʿaṣafat*) is said to have "broken/wrecked" a ship (*qaṣafat al-safīnah*).
Al-Ṭirimmāḥ is cited using this image of Tamīm: they talk boldly of war but, when it comes, are "brittle as canes," their weakness showing.
The lexicographers derive qurʾ from qaraʾa = "to gather/collect,"
Al-qirāʾa is the joining of letters and words to one another in measured recitation (tartīl).
أَقْرَأْتُ فلاناً = "I made someone recite" (cf. Q 87:6, "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget")
In Q 17:78, "the qurʾān of dawn" means its recitation.
with Ibn ʿAbbās glossing: "when We have gathered it and fixed it in your heart, act by it."
The Prophetic saying "refrain from prayer during the days of your aqrāʾ" means the days of menstruation
a single origin: blackness, i.e. the opposite of whiteness in colour
Verb forms: اسْوَدَّ / سَوَادَّ, "it became black."
Others rejected any link with forbearance and derived it instead from sense 2: a man is called sayyid because people take refuge in his sawād, his person.
The two senses are linked by the idea of breaking: to tabbara something is to smash it to pieces and so annihilate it.
tabār — destruction, perishing; and the verb tabbara — to shatter and destroy.
A verse of poetry plays on the contrast: other clans are cast from mere ore (tibr), while the Banū ʿAbd Manāf are gold.
al-Zajjāj: "save in destruction"; and it is precisely because of this breaking-sense that anything shattered is called tibr.
al-Zajjāj: tatbīr is demolition; anything you have broken and crumbled to pieces you have tabbara-ed.
a literal core of "heavy load / weighing down,"
وَقْر (waqr) in the ear = heaviness, hardness of hearing
وِقْر (wiqr) is a load one carries; plural أَوْقَار (awqār).
وَقَّرَ (form II) = to treat someone as weighty — to magnify him and not make light of him.
Verse cited: "How much foul speech my ear has been deafened against, though there is no deafness in me."
one single root meaning covering, and mingling under a cover
خَمْر (khamr) — the well-known drink.
خِمَار (khimār) — a woman's head-covering; خِمْرَة is the manner of wearing it (a woman "good in her khimra").
Abū Dhuʾayb's line describes men caught unawares, "like the birds of the covert."
Proverb: "the matron is not taught how to wear the head-covering," i.e. the experienced need no instruction.
yanaʿa/yayniʿu and the more common aynaʿa/yūniʿu both mean fruit "matured and ripened" (adraka wa-naḍija).
The ripe fruit itself is called yāniʿ, and the abstract noun is al-yanʿ ("ripening, maturity").
ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib comparing teeth to "ripe pomegranate" (rummān yanīʿ)
highlights.note: ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib, lived into Islam

highlights.text: Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī describing a scent "from ripe [fruit] moist with dew."
The root sense of zakāh is growth arising from God's blessing (baraka).
"Zakā al-zarʿu yazkū" is said of a crop when it grows and prospers.
zakiyy means made pure by creation.
the name for what a person gives from God's due to the poor
Zāla, yazūlu, zawālan: a thing leaves its course, veering away from it.
The word is used of something that was previously fixed in place.
gives their meaning as that of mā bariḥtu ("I did not cease")
Another line reads: "whenever she sees us, her zawīl departs from her."
a single core idea: **laying something flat over something else of its own kind, so as to cover it.**
*ṭabaq* = *ḥāl* (condition). He cites Q 84:19, *la-tarkabunna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq* — "you shall mount stage upon stage."
Shāhid: Imruʾ al-Qays on rain — a steady, long-fringed drizzle that is "a covering of the earth," seeking its mark and pouring.
breadth, expanse, spreading out.
a disease/ailment.
The sea (al-baḥr) is named for its istibḥār — its spreading out and vastness.
baḥartu l-nāqa = to slit a she-camel's ear; such a camel is the baḥīra. Pre-Islamic Arabs did this after her tenth birth, then left her unridden and unused.
tabaḥḥara l-rāʿī = the shepherd ranging over wide pasture (cited from a verse of Umayya)
balawtu: to try/test someone (he proved "the best of those tried")
buliya / ubtuliya bi-: to be tried or afflicted; baliyya / balwā: a calamity that befalls one
God tries the servant with a good or bad trial
Hence lā ubālīhi, "I do not reckon with him," from not troubling to inform oneself about him (Zuhayr: "she does not care")
Hadith: refuge is sought from the hardship of balāʾ — except a balāʾ that carries elevation of rank with God.
the hamzated form yields a single root: repelling / pushing away.
From this same idea of "knowing where the quarry is" comes دَرَى in the sense of knowing/perceiving: دَرَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I knew the thing"), أَدْرانِيهِ اللهُ ("God made me know it").
Ibn Fāris cites Q 10:16, {…nor would He have made you know of it} (walā adrākum bihi)
الدَّرِيئَة: the practice-ring for spear-thrusting (verse of ʿAmr)
f-r-sh as a single sound root whose core idea is smoothing something out and spreading it flat.
Base sense — spreading. فَرَشْتُ الفِرَاشَ ("I spread the bedding").
الفَرْش of livestock — animals fit only for slaughter and eating.
فَرَاش is the flying insect (moth/butterfly), so named for its lightness.
a line of Abū Duʾād describing a scout who "came running with the fluttering of the ostrich, at a sprint, the day already high."
On the saying "the child belongs to the firāsh," he reports that some took firāsh to mean the husband, while arguing that strictly the firāsh is the woman, since she is the one bedded
derives the root ف ر ض (f-r-ḍ) from the concrete idea of a notch or incision
He reads the Qur'anic naṣīban mafrūḍan as "an apportioned, delimited share,"
faraḍat / faruḍat al-baqara: the cow grew old and advanced in years — al-Jawharī connects this to the Qur'anic lā fāriḍun wa-lā bikr ("neither aged nor young").
cited from Labīd, "as the Euphrates flows over the outlet of the streamlet."
with a verse from Ṣakhr al-Ghayy, and the note that one must not read the word as qirṣ)
al-farḍ is what God has made obligatory

Al-Aʿshā uses the plural, quṭūṭ, in a line on King al-Nuʿmān "giving out the quṭūṭ" on the day the poet met him.
those who said it meant, as it were, the documents of reward they are given in the Hereafter
one family built on the number "four" and its derivatives
أربعة (four), أربعون (forty), رُبع (a quarter), رُباع (four at a time)
a single root whose core idea is throwing, pelting, or flinging
الرَّدَى is destruction; رَدِيَ يَرْدَى = "he perished"; أَرْدَاهُ اللَّهُ = "God destroyed him."
التَّرَدِّي is plunging into a chasm
one single, regular meaning: assisting and backing someone by giving — a gift or other support
الرَّفْد (al-rafd) is the verbal noun of "rafadahu" — he gave him [something]
"Urfidtu al-māl" — I was given/granted the wealth
Ibn Fāris cites a line of al-Farazdaq mentioning "Iraq and its two Rāfids."
A ḥadīth uses it: "the fayʾ [war-gained wealth] becomes rifd"
one central image — the leg/foot (rijl) of any creature that has one
الرِّجْل (al-rijl) — the leg/foot of a human or animal
foot-soldiers/infantry (al-rajjāla), so named because they travel on their feet
الرَّجُل (al-rajul) — a "man," a single adult male
Cited verse: a vow to visit "the House of God, on foot and barefoot."
**flinging or casting a thing away**
رَمَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَرْمِيهِ — "I threw (or shot at) the thing, I throw it."
"going in search of something" — a compound notion combining *going* and *seeking*.
Al-sa'āma is weariness/tedium that comes from something continuing too long
Supporting verse of poetry: "I have grown weary of life's burdens; whoever lives eighty years grows weary"
the succession of many things, each connected to the next
glossed as ensuring the proportion between rivet and hole is exact, neither too tight nor too loose
al-sard — a collective term for chainmail and similar ring-linked work
وَرى (with fatḥa; also the dialectal wariya with kasra) = to produce/give out fire
وارَيْتُ الشيءَ = I hid the thing; تَوارى = he hid himself
وَراءَ (warāʾ) = "behind," but can also mean "in front / ahead,"
Al-Jawharī reads the Qurʾānic "and behind them was a king" (18:79) as meaning "ahead of them."
a single governing sense, which he takes from al-Khalīl: **concealing something**
خَدَعْتُ الرجل — "I deceived the man," glossed as ختلته (I tricked / caught him off guard)
Cited proverb: «الحرب خُدَعة» ("war is trickery")
"to increase, grow, add, exceed"
Of a thing growing of itself: زاد ("increased") — of water or wealth
Of causing growth: God "increased him in wealth"
Of exceeding: "he exceeded what he intended"
Cited from Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī: "you are a company exceeding a hundred; so gather your whole affair and scheme against me"
the governing sense (taʾwīl) of baʿth as the removal of whatever was holding something back from acting or moving
highlights.note: Ibn Sīda's governing sense of baʿth

highlights.text: To send. بَعَثَهُ (baʿathahu) = to send someone on his own
بَعَثَ اللهُ الخلق, which Ibn Sīda glosses as nasharahum
highlights.note: God raising creation, as in the Qur'an

highlights.text: illustrated by a line of Ḥumayd b. Thawr on a careworn man kept sleepless by his worries
highlights.note: Ḥumayd b. Thawr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: a single root whose core idea is one thing encircling or surrounding another from its sides
**دَارَتْ بِهِمُ الدَّوَائِر** — "adverse turns of fortune encircled them," i.e., disliked conditions surrounded them.
The base verb is دَارَ / يَدُورُ (to turn, revolve), verbal noun دَوَرَان.
Cited: "and time, with man, is ever-turning."
Ibn Fāris cites two prophetic ḥadīths using dūr/dār for tribes
a single sound root whose core notion is a thing flowing or running easily
فَاضَ الْمَاءُ (fāḍa al-māʾ), "the water overflowed."
أَفَاضَ الْقَوْمُ مِنْ عَرَفَةَ, "the people poured forth from ʿArafa," i.e. they pushed off in a body
أَفَاضَ الْقَوْمُ فِي الْحَدِيثِ, "they launched into the conversation," i.e. threw themselves into it
أَعْطَاهُ غَيْضًا مِنْ فَيْضٍ, "he gave him a ghayḍ out of a fayḍ," glossed as "a little out of much."
The core idea running through the whole entry is covering / enveloping (taghṭiya).
(yughshī al-layl al-nahār) "He covers the night with the day"
ghashiyahu al-amr / taghashshāhu = the affair enveloped him
All mean "a covering" (ghiṭāʾ).
Ibn Sīda cites Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba al-Ḥārithī: "We share our swords with them in the worst division: ours the coverings, theirs the edges."
the al-ghāshiya is glossed either as the Resurrection (it envelops all creation) or as the Fire (it envelops the faces of the deniers)
a single sound root whose core notion is one thing gripping or clinging to another with force
الكَلْب (al-kalb), the familiar animal
الكَلَّاب (al-kallāb) and المُكَلِّب (al-mukallib) are terms for the man who trains a dog to hunt
"we paid for our slain with the like of them, and with uncounted shackled captives"
Ibn Fāris identifies one core meaning for this root, with two intertwined strands: gathering/collecting, and nearness/closeness.
Kathīb (كَثِيب), "sand dune" — a heap of sand, again from the idea of things gathered together.
A line of poetry by al-Nābighah is cited, describing spears displayed "above the kawāthib" (i.e., held up over the horses' withers).
a single sound root whose core idea is passing one thing over another with a flat, spreading motion — wiping, stroking, smoothing
to pass the hand (or something) flat over a surface — "I wiped/stroked it with my hand" (masaḥtuhu bi-yadī, verbal noun masḥ)
whose single unifying idea is taraddud — repeated back-and-forth motion, surging or wavering movement
a she-camel "tamūru" (sways/surges) as she moves, and is called "mawwāra," swift
"Al-mawr" as wave — the surging swell of water.
Ṭarafa's ode is quoted describing such a camel
Striking / hollowing out / decay
Scooping / ladling
Qadaḥa, in its basic sense, means to strike or gouge into something
The verb also covers striking fire (qadaḥtu l-nār)
measuring or estimating one thing against another
Al-qaws = the dhira', a forearm-length unit of measurement — named this because it is the standard by which something is measured. The same word names the qaws, the archer's bow.
Cited: a verse of Imru' al-Qays on women not loving a poor or grey-haired, stooped man.
the exegetes gloss this as "two forearm-lengths."
taking something swiftly and by snatching it away
Basic sense — stripping/snatching: salabtuhu thawbahu ("I stripped/snatched his garment from him").
He quotes Labīd's line mentioning "the black sulub-garments... and the amsāḥ [coarse cloth]."
A hadith is cited: "Whoever kills a [combatant] in battle, the salab [the slain man's weapons and gear] belongs to him."
al-salwa — a bird identified with quail (al-suman)
Illustrated with a line of poetry by Ru'bah
Al-thayyib, applied to a woman, is one who married and then separated from her husband — by any means — after he had had intercourse with her.
God's words "thayyibātin wa-abkāran" (Q. 66:5) — "previously-married women and virgins"
"The two thayyibs are stoned; the two virgins (bikrs) are flogged and exiled"
a single root with one core idea: the falling / dropping of something
وَقَعَ الشَّيْءُ وُقُوعًا — "the thing fell/occurred"; the active participle is وَاقِعٌ ("falling, befalling")
الْوَاقِعَة — "that which befalls,"
"everything you gather and carry, you have wasaqtahu."
"The moon ittasaqa" — became full/complete, its light aligned into wholeness.
"wa'l-layli wa-mā wasaq" — "by the night, and what it wasaq [gathers/enshrouds]"
Labīd uses this in a verse describing a garden: on the day provision became abundant, the palms were mūsiqāt (heavily laden) and other growth was copious and first-yielding.
Core sense — the colour green.
الخُضْرة is the familiar colour.
The saying "Beware the greenery of the dung-heaps" is applied to a beautiful woman of bad origin
**snatching something away quickly and lightly**
الخَطْف = snatching away
بَرْقٌ خَاطِفٌ — lightning described as snatching away the light of the eyes.
The shayṭān "snatches" hearing, i.e. steals it furtively.
Cited from al-Nābigha: "crooked hooks on stout ropes, drawn toward you by hands pulling hard."
two base senses: (1) proportioning/measuring out a thing, and (2) smoothness of a thing
خُلُق (khuluq) = inborn disposition or temperament (السجية), so called because its possessor has been "proportioned"/determined upon it.
الخَلَاق (al-khalāq) = one's allotted share or portion, because each person's share has been apportioned to him.
Zuhayr's line contrasting one who "cuts out what he has measured"
some take the word as a reduplicated form belonging with the weak roots, from zāḥa, yazīḥu, "to draw back"
Others say it is taken from al-zawḥ, "hard driving", and likewise al-dhawḥ.
glossing zuḥziḥa as "moved aside and put at a distance"
zaḥḥahu and zaḥzaḥahu: he pushed him and moved him from his place, and put him at a distance from it
From zāḥa come Labīd's line "he drew back (zāḥa) from a stand like mine, and moved away"
"Whoever fasts a day in the way of God, God will move him (zaḥzaḥahu) seventy autumns away from the Fire"
zafara (yazfuru): to pant/groan with a heavy exhalation, like the groan of a mother who has lost a child (zafrat al-thaklā). The noun for this groaning sound is zafīr.
Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line is cited: an inherited glory "whose zawāfir have not failed it."
whose core notion is **putting at a distance, driving away**
طَرَدْتُهُ ṭaradtuhu — "I drove him away."
With the ruler as subject, forms IV and II (أَطْرَدَهُ / طَرَّدَهُ) mean to banish someone from his town
Do you recognise a trace, like the running-on of streaked patterns, belonging to ʿAmra — desolate, save for a rider's halting-place?
treats b-r-d as having four independent bases, with all derived forms tracing back to one of them
barada / bārid: to be cold, cold.
saḥāb barid: a cloud carrying hail (barad).
a verse promises a she-camel that "will cool livers and set mourners weeping."
evidenced by a verse on gazelles pillowed on the arṭā bush's "two cool sides."
treats d-n-w as nearness (al-dunūw = al-qurb), whether nearness in essence or nearness in status and judgement
The palm tree's "clusters hanging near" (qinwān dāniya, Q 6:99) show the plain sense.
**First**, against "last": al-dunyā against al-ākhira
adnā means it is nearer, for their own souls, to aiming at justice in testifying
In the saying "when you eat, fa-dannū", al-Rāghib derives the word from al-dūn ("what is near/below"), giving the sense "eat from what is next to you"
treats j-d-r as two independent roots
جِدَار (jidār) = a wall; plurals جُدُر (judur) and جُدْرَان (judrān)
هو جَدِيرٌ بكذا (huwa jadīrun bi-kadhā), "he is fit/worthy of it,"
derives every sense of the root ج-ل-س (j-l-s) from one core meaning: rising/elevation (al-irtifāʿ)
jalasa describes the transition from lying down or sleep into a sitting position
several lines of poetry (al-Hudhalī and others) using jalasa/al-jālis in this "went up to Najd" sense
turns on "coming into being / being brought forth" and, from that, "growing up."
"God brought creation forth (anshaʾa), so it came to be (nashaʾū)."
Qur'anic phrase "الجوار المنشآت" — the running ships with sails hoisted.
with the Qur'anic phrase "من ينشّؤا في الحلية" ("one reared amid ornament")
A verse of al-Shammākh uses mustanshaʾāt ("raised-up things") of howdah-like shapes
a single sound root whose core sense is: striking something until a dent or hollow is beaten into it
naqīr: the small speck on the back of a date-stone
He cites a woman's saying to her husband: take me past the men of naẓarā (who look) but not past the women of naqarā (who backbite)
God would not leave off from the slayer of a believer, i.e. not desist from punishing him
قَصَا – يَقْصُو – قُصُوّاً is to move away or stand apart, said of anything
القاصية (al-qāṣiya) describes both people and places that are remote and set apart
Ruʾba: "it leaves the soil of the deserts with its dust-clouds driven wild."
hanging something on something so that it stays attached to it
a share, a portion
taqlīd — putting a mark on the neck.
maqālīd — said to mean treasuries or storehouses
Ibn Fāris cites the poet Bishr: "Your patron bestowed it on you out of rancour — and Jaʿfar was collared with it as with a dove's ring-collar."
sets out three genuine base-meanings for this root
Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 22:21, "wa-lahum maqāmiʿu min ḥadīd" ("for them are maces of iron")
He quotes the pre-Islamic/early poet Aws (ibn Ḥajar): God sent down His help, while the dust-colored gazelles in their lairs go on warding off flies (taqammaʿu).
A ḥadīth calls certain people "the funnels of speech" (aqmāʿ al-qawl): those who hear but retain nothing, as if their ears were funnels that hold nothing back
whose single idea is: mingling with a thing, getting entangled in it, and putting it on like a garment
اقْتَرَفَ (iqtarafa) = to acquire or gain something
a people complained of the pestilence of their land and were told, "Move away, for from al-qaraf comes destruction."
two sound root meanings: cold, and firm establishment (settling in place)
Qarra and istaqarra: to settle, to become settled
may God give him enough that his eye rests and does not look longingly to anyone above him
Imruʾ al-Qays: "when they mount the horses and put on their mail, the earth burns, though the day is cold (qarr)."
a single consistent root meaning breadth/spaciousness and moving out freely across the land
سَرَب / سَرِب (sarab, sarib) — water leaking or flowing from a water-skin
سَارِب (sārib) — one going forth openly in the land
Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, "What ails your eye that water pours from it, as though it were a leak from the split seams of a water-skin"
sāḥa al-māʾ describes water flowing/streaming over the ground
sāḥa fī al-arḍ means to travel or roam through the land (siyāḥa)

to join/connect one thing to another (waṣala … fa-ttaṣala, "he joined it, and it became joined")
Form II waṣṣala (tawṣīl) = to splice or link repeatedly; cited with Qurʾān 28:51, "We have joined together the discourse for them."
a ewe that "accompanied"/was paired with her brother among the flock's young and so was spared slaughter
ittaṣala / waṣala ilā a tribe = to attach oneself, claim lineage (verse of al-Aʿshā)
khaṭṭa al-kitāb — to write a document
wa lā takhuṭṭuhu bi-yamīnika" — "nor did you write it with your right hand"
illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah about an unmatched rival at the Battle of ʿUkāẓ
derives the whole root خ-ب-ط from one core idea: treading and striking
the verb يَتَخَبَّطُ here carries the same "being struck/buffeted" image
treats خ-ر-ق as a single root meaning to tear something open and to cut/pass through it
The poet Dhū al-Khiraq al-Ṭuhawī got his name from his line "upon it are the feathers and the rags."
An Arab saying: "She has neither a height that disparages her nor a shortness that abashes her"
al-yaqīn is knowledge that removes doubt and settles a matter as certain — the opposite of doubt, as knowledge is the opposite of ignorance
all meaning "to be/become certain of a matter"
al-yaqan = al-yaqīn, with a shāhid from al-Aʿshā
glossed as "until death comes to you," i.e. worship Him always, to the point of death
z-h-q as one root meaning: to move forward, to pass on, to go past a limit
زَهَقَتْ نَفْسُهُ — "his soul departed."
زَهَقَ الْبَاطِلُ — falsehood zahaqa, glossed by him simply as "it passed away, went off."
Shāhid from Zuhayr, contrasting the mounts of a war-leader: "among them the lean and among them the fat, grease-laden (al-zāhiq al-zahim)."
derives ṭ-r-f from two distinct roots: (1) the edge or border of a thing, and (2) a movement of the eyelids
ṭaraf = the edge/tip of a thing, a garment, or a wall
originally the movement of the eyelids in looking; by extension it also names the eye itself
eyes with a languorous "sickness" in their glance slay their lovers yet do not revive them
Opposite of light.
Putting a thing out of its proper place, wrongfully.

cited with Kaʿb's line ("...and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong")

treats b-q-y as a single root meaning permanence / enduring (al-dawām)
baqiyya / buqyā = sparing, clemency, mercy shown to someone

treats B–W–L as two separate roots: (1) fluid that seeps or flows out; (2) al-rūʿ — the inner part of a person into which a thought falls
مَا خَطَرَ بِبَالِي, "it never crossed my bāl," glossed as "it was not cast into my rūʿ (inward self)."
a wineskin that bursts and gushes its drink; attested in ʿAdī's poetry
Ibn Muqbil's verse uses the phrase for the mirage of the Ḥimyarī uplands
He cites Ibn ʿAbbās, asked about performing wuḍūʾ with milk: "I do not mind it in the least; be easy and you will be dealt with easily."
one core idea: to incline or draw something toward yourself by means of a sound or speech that you produce

Shāhid: a line of Imruʾ al-Qays ("...the people do not claim that I flee")
doubled d-r points to two root meanings: one thing issuing from another, and agitation (unsteady movement) in a thing
darra is the pouring of clouds, and clouds of abundant rain are midrār
the piercing, shining star, likened to durr and named after it for its whiteness
al-Hudhalī's verse on a pearl over which "the sweet water lingers and surges"
going ahead in order to guide.
sending a kindness.
هَدَيْتُهُ الطَّرِيقَ ("I guided him on the road") = I went ahead to direct him
الْهُدَى (right guidance) as the opposite of الضَّلَالَة (going astray)
الْهَدِيَّة (a gift) = a kindness sent to someone one loves
A verse of poetry illustrates a spear-point as a man's "guide" through the land.
resting on two root meanings: cutting, and the drawing-together of a thing
al-jubb is a well.
Abū Khirāsh, describing an eagle that lifts its prey and then lets it drop, says the prey "struck the hard ground (al-jabūb) with the place between its eyes"
the root has one core meaning: cutting (al-qaṭʿ)
arḍ juruz is land with no vegetation, as if growth had been cut off from it
Ash-Shammākh's line is cited describing a rasp in the nasal passage and nostrils.
"A hating woman will not be satisfied except with a jarzah"
one core meaning: turning/rotation, and by extension, gathering into a mass
as though the sun were entirely gathered/bundled up
He wraps/turns the one over the other and the other over the one
means to turn away and swerve off from God's dīn

A line of Ḥumayd ibn Thawr: "Enough for me of supporting the two Khubaybs, enough / the leader is not the miserly, deviating one (al-mulḥid)."

The proverb "huwa sharrābun bi-anquʿ" — "he is a drinker at [hidden] pools" — describes someone who repeats a matter over and over
naqaʿa al-ṣawt — a sound rose up, illustrated with a line of poetry about a war-cry gathering people for battle
this root carries two core meanings: (1) aiming/purposing toward something, and (2) the stone/pit of something
al-nawā meaning "the pit of a date."
analyzes ق ن ع as containing two distinct core ideas, plus a possible third
al-qāniʿ being "the one who begs," so called because he turns toward the person he's asking
iqnāʿ meaning "raising something up with no downward dip."

which the exegetes explained as "raising their heads."
a single core sense: one thing rising or mounting upon another
رَكِبَ (rakiba, "he rode/mounted")
الرِّكَاب (al-rikāb): riding-camels
الرَّكْب (al-rakb) and الْأُرْكُوب (al-urkūb): a riding party
one root whose single underlying idea is bewilderment or disorientation (ḥayra)
سُكْر (sukr) is the drunkenness produced by drink
{إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا} — "our eyes have merely been sukkirat", i.e. dazed

a verse by Mālik b. Zaghba al-Bāhilī on aversion arriving "so soon" while the bond of union frays
وهب (wahaba) — to give something as a gift
al-Wahhāb "the abundant in gifts."
Al-wasan and al-sinah (this author treats سِنَة as belonging to the same root) both name a light doze or drowsiness that overtakes a person
a verse by Ḥumayd ibn Thawr in which a rain-cloud "visits" a meadow the way a night-phantom visits a sleeper
highlights.note: Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, lived into Islam

al-khaymah ("tent") — well known; explicitly named for the fact that one resides (aqāma) in/at it
Supported by a line of poetry describing "a stacked frame of tent-poles" left standing [of an abandoned camp]
One sound root: elevation, rising, loftiness, and fullness/abundance.
al-farʿ — the top/highest part of a thing
illustrated with a line of poetry by Aws comparing a dull-witted man to such a swaddled calf
treats it under the core idea of "leaning / inclining,"

with a verse of al-Namir on hastening a she-camel "when the late afternoon declined."

Ibn Muqbil (the two time-spans passing over ruins, wearing them with decay)

is, at root, "increase over the capital."
